definition: Simulate means to reproduce the appearance or workings of something — to produce a convincing stand-in for the real thing without being it.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word simulate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know simulate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The hoverfly cannot sting, but its yellow-and-black bands simulate a wasp so convincingly that birds give it the same wide berth.
Mimic is lighter than simulate: a mimic copies the look or sound of a thing in the moment, while simulating rebuilds its whole behavior — conditions, responses, and all.
Counterfeit goes further than simulate: a simulation is openly an imitation, but a counterfeit is built to be taken for the genuine article — imitation pushed all the way into fraud.

To mimic is to copy the look or sound of something in the moment — a comedian mimics a senator's drawl, a lyrebird mimics a chainsaw. To simulate is to rebuild the thing's whole behavior: conditions, responses, consequences, usually so they can be studied or practiced.

To replicate is to produce an exact duplicate — the same experiment, the same result, the same object again. To simulate is to produce a convincing stand-in: the flight never leaves the ground, and nobody needs it to, because behaving like the real thing is the entire job.

Before email, wire photos and page proofs traveled by facsimile machine — the fax — curling out of the roller one warm sheet at a time.
Simulate means to reproduce the appearance or workings of something — to produce a convincing stand-in for the real thing without being it.

Before the crew ever touches the real spacecraft, they log four hundred hours in a mock-up that simulates it down to the switch guards — the cabin tilts, the instruments fail on cue, and the windows play footage of the turning Earth.
The mock-up is not a spacecraft and never pretends to leave the ground.
To simulate is to reproduce the conditions and behavior of the real thing so faithfully that practice inside the copy transfers to the original — imitation built for use, not for deceit.
Simulate is morally neutral machinery: flight crews, economists, and epidemiologists all simulate, and nobody blames them, because a simulation announces itself as an imitation.

The deception words in this unit begin exactly where that announcement stops — feign is a person faking their own state, counterfeit is imitation built to be taken for the genuine article, and legerdemain hides the imitation altogether.
Keep simulate for the honest copy: real behavior, openly reproduced, usually so something can be tested or practiced safely.

On Tuesday afternoons, the medical school's east ward admits twelve patients who are not sick.

They are trained actors, and the ward exists to simulate the worst hour of a residency: one 'patient' seizing, another quietly slipping into shock, a third demanding a diagnosis at the top of his voice.
Monitors display vitals scripted in a control room; the crash cart is stocked; the clock is real.
Students know none of it is genuine and sweat anyway, because the ward reproduces how an emergency behaves — its pacing, its noise, its decisions — without ever putting a life at risk.
Errors made on Tuesday, the dean likes to say, are the cheapest ones the hospital sells.
